prayer.text: Pope Saint Fabian, pray for us.

cues.text: A Newcomer Among Notables
According to the early historian Eusebius, Fabian was a layman who had simply come to Rome from the countryside to witness the election following the death of Pope Anterus in 236.
Among the illustrious and well-connected churchmen being seriously considered for the papacy, Fabian, Eusebius says, "was in the mind of none."
The Sign of the Dove
As the electors deliberated over several days, a dove is said to have suddenly descended and settled on Fabian's head.
For those gathered, the sight immediately recalled the Gospel scene of the Holy Spirit descending on Christ at his baptism.
Taking this as a sign of divine choice, the assembly elected the unknown newcomer pope with, in the Catholic Encyclopedia's words, 'joyous unanimity.'
Fourteen Years of Peace
Fabian's fourteen-year pontificate, unusually long and largely peaceful for the era, allowed him to organize the growing Roman Church in lasting ways.
He divided the city into seven ecclesiastical districts, each overseen by a deacon, and appointed notaries to collect and preserve official records of earlier martyrs' trials.
In doing so, he preserved history that would otherwise have been lost.
Missionary and Diplomatic Work
Tradition credits Fabian with sending seven missionary bishops into Gaul around 245, among them St. Denis , who would become the first bishop of Paris.

He also corresponded respectfully with the great biblical scholar Origen and, according to St. Cyprian , formally condemned a Bishop Privatus of Lambaesa for heresy in North Africa — evidence of a pope already exercising a wide, supervisory authority across distant provinces.
Reburial of Pontian and Hippolytus
It fell to Fabian to bring the story of his predecessors' reconciliation to its proper conclusion.
He arranged for the remains of Pope Pontian and the reconciled antipope Hippolytus , both of whom had died in Sardinian exile years earlier, to be recovered and buried with honor in Rome.
This formally closed the wound of that old schism.
Martyrdom Under Decius
The long peace ended abruptly in 250 with the accession of Emperor Decius .

He launched the first empire-wide, systematically enforced persecution of Christians, requiring inhabitants to sacrifice to the Roman gods under threat of severe penalties, which could include imprisonment, torture, or death.

Fabian was among its earliest and most prominent victims, martyred on January 20, 250, and buried in the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callistus, the very cemetery his own predecessor Callistus I had once overseen.
Legacy
Fabian's pontificate is remembered both for the memorable legend of his election and for the practical, organizational foundations he laid for the Roman Church.
These foundations were established during a rare stretch of calm and would prove essential within his own lifetime, as the Church faced the far harsher trials of the Decian persecution.
